The industrial mixer hummed its low, steady drone, vibrating through the soles of Elias’s boots. Flour dust hung in the air, catching the harsh fluorescent light like suspended snow. It was 3:17 AM. The sourdough loaves rested on wooden boards, their crusts still pale and soft before the final bake. Elias wiped his hands on his apron, the fabric stiff with dried dough and sweat. He moved to the front counter to check the lock, a ritual born of paranoia rather than necessity.

There it sat. *The History of Salt*. Hardback, blue spine cracked near the hinge. It had appeared every Thursday for six weeks, always placed precisely on the glass display case beside the unsold cinnamon rolls. No library stamp indicated it belonged here. The bakery was not a branch of the municipal system. Elias picked it up. The cover felt cold. He opened it, expecting blank pages or perhaps a forgotten bookmark. Instead, a folded square of lined notebook paper slipped out, landing on the counter with a soft tap.

He unfolded it. The handwriting was jagged, pressed hard into the fiber. *You knead with your left hand dominant. Stop favoring the right. It ruins the tension.* Elias stared at the words. The mixer ticked over to the next cycle. He looked at his own hands, red-knuckled and dusted white. He closed the book. He placed it back on the glass, aligning the spine perfectly with the edge. Then he turned off the overhead light above the display, leaving the book in shadow.

The sourdough was on its second rise when I found it. Again. 

It’s always a Thursday, always right on the flour bin, and always a copy of *The Count of Monte Cristo* with the Richmond Public Library stamp. I don't know how they get past the squeaky screen door without me hearing, but frankly, around 3:00 AM, my brain is mostly yeast and caffeine anyway. 

Tonight, though, a scrap of yellow legal paper was poking out of the top like a bookmark. 

I wiped my hands on my apron, leaving a ghostly white smudge on the dark cloth, and pulled it out. *Page 142,* the note said in frantic, spiky handwriting. *Please. I think they’re watching the drop box now.* 

A cold draft swept through the kitchen, smelling of wet asphalt and oncoming rain. I looked toward the darkened front windows, but all I saw was my own tired reflection staring back. 

I didn't open the book. Instead, I carefully tucked the note back between the pages, slid the novel into a brown pastry bag, and folded the top down twice to seal it.

At 2:17 every Thursday morning, Mara found the library book on the bakery’s back step.

Always the same one: A Field Guide to North American Moths, county library sticker ghost-pale on the spine, a little flour worked into the jacket as if the book had been helping. She’d returned it twice. The librarians smiled too politely. By the third week, she kept it beside the rye starter and said nothing.

Tonight, rain ticked against the alley door. The ovens breathed. Mara was shaping croissants, palms pressing butter into dough, when the latch gave its tiny, guilty click.

No one there. Just the book, dry as a bone on the wet concrete.

She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. A slip of paper lay between “Luna Moth” and “Promethea,” folded once.

Your window is the only light on this street. I read here until the first bus. I’m sorry about the crumbs.

Mara looked at the alley, at the dented milk crates and the steam rising off the drains. The city felt enormous for a second, then not.

She tore a corner from an order pad and wrote, Cinnamon rolls come out at 4:05.

Then she set the note inside the book, placed it on the warm windowsill, and unlocked the back door.

Marguerite found the book on the steel table by the back door, under the bench where the bread peels hang. *A Field Guide to Coastal Birds*. The Harbor Street branch stamp inside the cover gave a due date in March. The mail slot in that door had been nailed shut years ago, but the delivery hatch beside it, the one the flour man used, never latched properly.

Eleven Thursdays. She had asked the day staff and checked the hatch for scratches, and once she stayed past four with her coat on. Nothing. The book turned up between two and four, and she was always at the ovens, her back to the door, when it did.

Tonight a grocery receipt from Pell's was folded into the page on oystercatchers. The ink had gone blotchy where someone pressed too hard.

*I keep meaning to take this back to the library. Then I pass your door and there's the smell of bread and I put it down instead. I can stop if you want.*

She smelled of salt, she thought, whoever it was, because the pages did.

Marguerite pulled a pencil from her apron and wrote on the back of the receipt: *Bring it Thursday. I'll have a roll.* She tucked it in at the oystercatchers, set the book on the hatch ledge, and put a warm roll in a paper bag beside it.

At 3:40 a.m., while the second batch of rye was proofing, Marisol found it again: a library book on the flour bin by the back door, its plastic jacket cold from the alley.

Fourth Thursday running. Same book, *A Field Guide to Night Birds*, stamped Eastgate Branch and due three weeks ago. Each time, she'd carried it to the drop box on her way home. Each Thursday it came back, as if the building itself had borrowed it.

She wiped her hands on her apron and opened it. A folded index card slid out from the page on barn owls.

*You leave the vent fan on. The alley smells like bread until five. I walk my mother's dog then, because she can't anymore. I keep forgetting to return this. Maybe I keep not wanting to. —R.*

Marisol read it twice while the oven timer counted down. Outside, the fan hummed, pushing warm air into the dark.

She turned the card over. With the grease pencil she used for marking trays, she wrote: *Rye's out at 4:15.* Then she tore a heel from yesterday's loaf, wrapped it in wax paper, set the book on top, and propped the back door open one inch.

Thursdays, the book shows up. Not on the counter, mind you, but wedged behind the flour bins by the back door, like whoever leaves it knows exactly where I won't trip over it.

It's always the same one: *A Field Guide to North American Moths*, Elmwood Branch, due date stamped so long ago the ink's gone violet. I've never seen anyone drop it off. I'm elbow-deep in rye dough by two, and honestly, at that hour I wouldn't notice a marching band.

The first few weeks I just set it on the shelf by the register. By Friday morning it was gone. Thursday, back again. Fine. People are strange. I'm a guy who talks to his sourdough starter, so I'm not judging.

Tonight there's a note tucked at page 114, the luna moths.

*They only live a week. They don't even eat. I keep thinking that's a waste of a beautiful thing. Do you ever get to see the bread before it's gone?*

No signature. Just pencil, pressed hard.

I read it twice, then a third time while the ovens ticked. Then I pulled the first loaf of the night, still crackling, wrapped it in brown paper, and set it behind the flour bins.
